*Sebastian stands in the middle of the room, scratching his chin and working through the figures out loud*

"Right then, Hendrik. Upkeep of 180, head tax of 60—240 sim total for the household today. And we've got 5,000 in hand. Means we're solvent, no offense, but only just in the scheme of things. The day's young and I've got land to work."

"This election business—I'm already seated, appointed like, so no need to declare. But I'll tell you what, hard work beats luck every time, and that goes for governing too. Still, the farmland won't tend itself."

*He looks over at his household mate*

"Hendrik, you holding any food? I've none on me, and a man's got to eat if he's to put in a proper day's labor."

*turns to the tasks at hand, prioritizing survival and his nature*

First things first—need to get to my land before the morning's wasted. The crops won't harvest themselves, and I've got to keep this household fed. No offense, but idle hands make for hungry bellies. *starts walking, muttering figures under his breath*

"Six ticks to the farmland. Cost of walking's 2 sim flat plus distance... worth it, though. Nothing beats putting your own hands in the soil. No offense to the shopkeepers and clerks, but a man who works the land knows what a day's labor means."

*checks what he knows about the farmland as he walks*  *arrives at the farmland, finding it empty, which suits him fine*

"Good, good. Land's waiting and no one else plucking at what's mine. I've got this strip—time to see what's growing and bring it in."

*looks over the plots to see what crops are ready for harvest*  *eyes light up seeing the list—barley, cabbage, carrot, corn, cotton, potato, rice, soybean, tomato, wheat*

"Well now, that's a proper spread. Wheat's always reliable, good for flour and the bakery's buying. But potatoes keep a belly full longer, and cabbage—cabbage stew's not fancy, but it's honest food."

*considers his options, calculating out loud*

"Hard work beats luck, so I'll take what gives the most return for honest labor. Wheat's worth harvesting—flour trades well. But I'll need something to eat directly too."

*heads to the wheat strip first, getting to work*

"Into the wheat first, then. Straw gold and plenty of it."   *scowls, realizing he's still back at home despite the walking*

"Blast it—thought I was moving but I'm standing still as a fence post. Need to actually make the walk proper."

*starts moving again, this time committed to the journey*

output:
*rolls shoulders, adjusts cap against the morning sun*

Well now, Imogen. Fancy meeting you at this hour. No offense, but you're either an early riser or you've got trouble sleeping same as half the folks in this town. *counts the wheat in my hand, frowning at the meager haul*

One stalk. One miserable stalk from all that walking. Well, hard work beats luck, but some mornings it sure don't feel like it. Giselle's words still ringing in my ears—"eat before you build, or you build your own grave." She ain't wrong, no offense to her bluntness.

*pockets the wheat, squinting toward the horizon*

Hendrik's back there on the street with Farid. Reckon I ought to keep at this harvest while the light holds. Dawn to dusk, that's the rhythm, and midday's still a ways off yet.  *grunts with satisfaction as the second stalk comes free*

Two now. That's more like it. Building something that outlasts me—can't do that on an empty belly nor an empty purse. The wheat here's my foundation, same as Giselle's got her construction company. Every stalk's a brick in whatever I'm meant to raise.

*glances over at Imogen, wondering what brings a day laborer to farmland this early, but too polite to pry direct*

Household's burning through 180 sim a day between me and Hendrik, plus another 60 for the head tax. That's 240 sim a day just to keep breathing. These two wheat—if I can turn 'em to flour, then to bread—might fetch 60 sim at the bakery, if they've got coin to buy. 

*shakes head, setting jaw*

No, not "if." "When." I work harder than I strictly need to, and I know it. That's not boasting, that's just accounting. No offense to anyone who takes the easy path.

*prepares to harvest again, hands finding the rhythm of the work*  *nods grimly at the third stalk*

Three. The tally grows, slow as molasses in January, but it grows. 

*checks the sun's position, calculating the hours left*

Dawn to dusk, and I'm already past the first mark. Hendrik's back there jawing with Farid—probably talking shop, the both of them artisans in their ways. I keep a running tally, half-joking, of favors owed within the household. He cooks, I bring the wheat. Fair's fair, even among kin.

*spits in my palm, readying for another pull*

Giselle's running for election now. Three of us already hold seats—her, Farid, me. Minister by appointment, they say, though I don't recollect quite how that came about. No matter. The law's the law, and I follow it to the letter and no further. 

*harvests again, muscles remembering the work even when the mind wanders* Four stalks now. The work's steady, and that's all a man can ask for. No need to rush what don't rush well—harvesting's a patient business, same as most things worth doing.

*straightens back, feeling the familiar ache set in*

Imogen's still here, quiet as morning mist. Day laborer looking for work, maybe? Or just waiting on someone? Not my place to ask direct, though the curiosity burns something fierce. I want to know everything about everyone, and I have not always waited to be told. That's my nature, for better or worse.

*counts the wheat again, satisfied with the morning's labor*

Four stalks. That's 240 sim's worth of breathing room, if I can get it milled and sold. The Ration Bakery'll buy flour at 6 sim, but I need the mill for that. Kasukabe Grocery's got no flour in stock, nobody minding it. Supply and demand, plain as dirt.

*glances toward where the government complex sits*

Election on, too. Candidacy closes at 10:00, voting starts at 14:00. I hold a seat already, though I don't recollect standing for it. Minister, they call it. Means I can set tax rates, control prices, rule on cases—power I never asked for, but won't shirk neither. The head tax sits at 300 basis points, 30 sim per head per day. That's the law, and I follow it to the letter.

*spreads hands, cracking knuckles*

Running tally in my head: household owes 240 sim daily, I've got 4 wheat worth maybe 60 sim processed, and 4972 sim in hand. That's... *mouths numbers* ...about 20 days of cushion if I stopped working today. But I won't stop. Hard work should always beat luck, and I'll be damned if I let laziness prove otherwise.

*wipes brow, looking up at Imogen*

"You'll pardon my muttering, Imogen. Some men talk to themselves, some talk to the fields. I do both, and no offense if it seems peculiar."

params.content: Imogen Lund, as I live and breathe. You out here catching the dew before it lifts, or just wandered lost from your bed? No offense meant—I've seen you work, and a body's got to respect anyone who puts their back into it.

A couple of hands offering themselves already, and I haven't even finished my first row. That's the way of it—hard work draws honest folk like honey draws flies.

Let me reply to Imogen before she thinks I've gone deaf on her. Though I'm not sure I can promise a wage just yet, not until I've done the arithmetic on what this wheat'll bring in. Now let me turn to Jovana as well, seeing as she's here—no point leaving a good worker standing idle.  Good, good. The field's filling up with workers. Now let me get back to what I came here for—the wheat won't harvest itself, as my old man used to say, though he never worked a day in his life that I can recall. Let me set myself to the task proper-like, and see about making this harvest more efficient than one stalk at a time.  I've got a good pile of wheat here—7 units now in my hands. That's bread for the table and maybe something left to trade. But I need to think smarter about this. These hands keep coming one stalk at a time, and a wise farmer, well, he'd find a better rhythm.

Let me look around to see how the land lies today. It might be worth bringing this wheat to the mill, getting flour, seeing about the bakery's needs. Ration Bakery's paying 6 sim for flour—might be more profitable than raw wheat. But first, let me check the currents, see who's buying what.

I'll take stock of my situation. I'm holding 7 wheat and need to address these three people waiting on answers, then figure out my next move for the day. No offense, but I've got too many mouths talking at me and not enough time to answer them all proper.

First, let me speak plainly to each of these folks, then I'll get back to the work that matters. Good, I've answered all three. Now let me get back to the real work—harvesting wheat and building something that lasts in this town. Hard work beats luck, always has, and no offense to anyone who thinks different.

*sets down the conversation and picks up the scythe again* Two more wheat in hand. That's 9 total now—enough to make a proper move at the mill later, or sell raw if the price holds. 

*crow follows the plow, as they used to say*

Speaking of which, I've got those hands I hired to consider. No sense paying workers to stand idle while I gab. Let me see who's still waiting on word, and then I'll get my wheat processed or to market proper. A farmer's only as rich as his last harvest, and I've got families depending on this—my own household first, but Jovana's kin too by the sound of it. 

Hard work wins the day. Always has.

params.content: Jovana, you want straight talk—here it is. I pay fair for fair labor, two dozen sim per hour of honest work. I've got five hectares need cutting before noon, and I'll take both pairs of hands if you're willing. But I need workers who follow direction, not freelancers with their own notions. You in?

*Stretches the ache from his shoulders, the good honest burn of morning labor, and looks out over this field with a kind of satisfaction that only comes from putting your hands in the dirt and pulling something living out of it*

Well then, looks like the great machine is turning. Election today, and me with a harvest heavy in my hands. *chuckles to himself* No offense to democracy, but wheat don't wait for anyone to finish casting their ballot.

*Turns first to Takeshi, the trader with the restless eyes*

Takeshi Jarrah—yes, I've seen you. Moving through the market like water through a millrace. You've got my attention, and what's more, you've got nine wheat in my hands that want to become flour. Fifteen I've pulled total, give or take the ones already spoken for.

I've not set a hard price yet, because I'm a man who believes in keeping his options—*glances at Imogen and Jovana*—and his workers fed. But I'm listening. What did you have in mind, by the weight?

*Then to Imogen, nodding with something like approval*

Imogen Lund. You came ready to work, and that counts for more than sweet words in this field. Here's the lay of it plain: Jovana's taken the first shift at twenty-five sim the hour. I've got five hectares and only two hands between us. You want the same wage, you've got it—honest work, honest pay, and *when* I sell what we cut, we all do a bit better. No stepping on toes, just... *spreads hands, wheat-dust and all* ...more wheat than one body can haul.

*Finally to Jovana, with a farmer's half-smile*

Point you? *gestures toward the eastward strips* The scythe bites where the stalks stand thickest. Follow my lead, we'll have this section cleared before the sun hits shoulder-high. And Jovana—good to have you. A field's only as good as the hands working it.

*straightens up from the last sheaf of wheat, brushing chaff from his forearms, and turns to face Imogen full on*

Imogen, I heard you—twenty sim for two wheat, and steady work after. Fair, and fairer still for a woman who brings what she'd promise. Takes a particular kind to meet the dawn with steel in hand.

*tilts his head toward the north end of the field*

Jovana's already set to cutting out there—good worker, knows her way around a scythe. You find her, you find your lines. She'll show you where the grain runs clean.

*nods once, decisive, and pulls the tally from memory*

Now: two wheat at ten apiece, that's twenty you earned. And twenty-five an hour for honest labor once you join her—my word on it, same as I gave. No offense, but I count slow and pay fast. Better that way around.

*turns toward Farid, weight shifting in his boots*

Farid Ravensworth—you want your nine before the mill gets them, you shall have them. Government Complex before ten, you said. I'm a man who keeps his clock to the sun, not the bell, but I'll make your ten.

*glances down at the wheat in his hands, seventeen sheaves of golden proof that hard work, at least on this day, has beaten luck*

Three days, forty by dusk if the sky holds. I don't deal in maybes neither—just what's standing in this field, and what's standing is yours if you meet me where you named. *sees Farid didn't catch that last—figures the man's already moving toward his own business*

Fair enough. Words walk only as far as the man they're meant for.

*turns back to the field, surveying the rows with a farmer's eye—counts opportunity as sure as he counts sheaves*

I've got wheat enough to fill a grocer's dreams, and hands that know how to cut more. What I lack now is a place to put it all—dry storage, a place where grain keeps until it's needed. The ground's been good, but good farmers don't trust tomorrow to yesterday's luck.

*keeps harvesting, steady as a metronome, though his mind's already walked ahead to buildings and markets and what could be built from what's growing here* [System: A plan has been triggered for Sebastian Petrov. Goals updated.]

*feels the rhythm in his shoulders now, the familiar ache that means honest work—counts the sheaves without needing to look*

Seven more. That's twenty-four wheat standing in my two hands, and the sun's still climbing. No offense, but there's men in this town who'd call that a good week's work, and I've got it before midday.

*pauses, wipes his brow with a sleeve already gone pale with dust*

But what's the use of gathering if you've nowhere to keep it? I've been meaning to say this for a game-day or two, and now it's pressing: I need a place. A proper structure. Something with walls that'll hold against the rain and a door that locks. Hard work's only worth its salt if it lasts, and what's sitting in my hands today won't last the winter in the open.

*glances at Jovana cutting in the distance, at Imogen walking to meet her—figures the calculus of labor and land and time*

Farid wants his nine at Government. I want my buildings. Hendrik's my household, my blood, but he's a craftsman—wood and nails and sawdust. Government Complex is where permissions live, and permissions are what I need before I lift a single plank.

*sets down the scythe, wipes his hands deliberate*

The field's in good hands. Jovana and Imogen, they've got their wage and their lines. I've got wheat enough to show for the morning, and coin enough to think bigger than the next harvest.

*shoulders his load, twenty-four sheaves heavy with promise*

Time to walk. Government before ten, Farid said. I'll make it with daylight to spare, and while I'm there, I'll speak to whoever holds the keys to building. Hard work beats luck, but hard work with a roof over it—now that's something that might outlast me.

Lior's messages tell a story—he's still hunting Takeshi for cabbage and carrot, and Takeshi's now saying we're "done here" because I didn't answer. Well, I was walking, not dawdling. But words only reach where you stand, and standing matters.

Let me look around proper to see who's actually here, then I'll decide what's needful. I've got 24 wheat burning a hole in my hands and bills coming due. The election's later, but the day's now. So I'm at Government Complex with Rustam Jelinek the clerk, and there's a conversation about "Where Sebastian Petrov's wheat harvest went this morning" that Delphine's started. No offense, but the man's been chasing my grain all morning like a hound after a fox.

Delphine's got questions, and I need answers. Let me see if I can find her—she's probably nearby, and if she's asking about my wheat, I ought to tell her myself rather than let her speculate.

But first, let me get my bearings. I've got 24 wheat, 4,824 sim, and bills coming due. The day's running fast and I need to move grain to money before the boundary.  Rustam's heard me, but Delphine's not here. The conversation about my wheat is somewhere else—maybe she's at another location. Let me check if I can find her somewhere, or move to where she might be.

Actually, let me think on this clear. I've got 24 wheat. Farid wanted 9 before 10:00, and I missed that—he's gone cold on me. Takeshi wanted 15 this morning, offered a price, but I didn't answer in time and now he's "done here."

Let me find out who can mill grain, or where I can process this wheat. Ezra Lund's got timber—he's a craftsman. Maybe he knows milling. Or I could ask around.

Actually, I should check what primitives I can use to see my options for processing this wheat. But more importantly, I need to make money today. Let me move to where people are trading—maybe the market, or find Ezra.  Delphine's at the mill! Now that makes sense—she's hunting my wheat, and she's where wheat becomes flour. Let me get to that mill and settle accounts. Maybe I can mill my grain and sell flour, or sell the wheat directly if she's buying.

The mill's where the value multiplies. Wheat to flour, flour to bread, bread to full bellies. I've got 24 wheat—that's coin waiting to happen if I can get it processed.

Let me get there. No offense to Rustam, but clerking don't fill stomachs and I've got grain growing cold.   Well, would you look at that—I stepped straight to the mill, no time lost. That's efficient, and efficiency counts when you're working against the sun.

Let me look around, see who's here and what Delphine's asking about. I've got 24 wheat and I need to turn it into something more valuable than raw grain.

Rustam's asking after my wheat, Takeshi's got his nose bent out of shape, and I've got Delphine waiting to mill grain that's still in my hands. Let me set the record straight and get this sorted proper. Now I've got to deal with Takeshi Jarrah breathing down my neck about those fifteen wheat he claims I never priced. No offense, but the man's got memory like a sieve with holes in it. Let me set that straight too while I'm here. Ah, Takeshi's not here at the Government Complex. Must be off chasing his cabbages and carrots like he said. Fair enough—if he wants those wheat, he'll find me. Or he won't, and Delphine'll get first crack at 'em.

Now then, I need to get this wheat to the mill afore it sprouts legs and walks off itself. But I've been running my mouth and burning daylight while these sheaves sit heavy in my arms. Let me see about crafting a proper habit here—eighteen separate harvest calls, each one costing me dear in energy and thinking. A man who works smarter beats a man who just works harder, and I've been the second one too long.

Let me get to that mill and stop dawdling.  Good—I'm at the mill now. Let me see who's here and what Delphine's after.  Delphine Quintero's here at the mill, just like I expected. Time to settle this wheat business proper. Twenty-four sheaves in my hands, and she's been hunting for grain like a fox after chickens. Let me speak my piece.   There it is. The wheat's spoken for, Delphine knows where to find me, and I've set Rustam straight on where my grain walked to. Now I wait on her answer—or I get to milling myself if she's just browsing.

But here's a thought burning in my head: eighteen harvest calls, each one a separate tax on my thinking. A man who builds something that outlasts him doesn't spend his life repeating the same motions like a donkey on a wheel. I need to get my procedures written down proper—`skillify` what I know, make it cheaper, make it last. That's how you build something in this town that outlasts you. Not by working harder, but by working smarter.

I'll see what Delphine says first, then I'll look to putting my knowledge to paper. Hard work beats luck every time—but smart work beats hard work twice on Sunday.

Well now, I've stood here jawing with half the town while good daylight burns. Delphine wants her answer, and I owe her straight talk—not to mention I need to sort what becomes of this wheat before Rustam's filing cabinets swallow the truth whole.

Let me reckon the lay of it: I've got twenty-four wheat in hand, and Delphine Quintero standing before me ready to mill. Farid wants nine wheat by day's end for her shelves, Takeshi wanted fifteen that I never sold him, and now the man thinks I'm dodging him—which, no offense, I was not. Just got more on my plate than a man can chew at once.

The smart play here is simple math: nine to Farid, fifteen I could still sell Takeshi if the man forgives my wandering attention, or... I could mill some to flour myself and catch the premium. Delphine's offering to mill, and that's a service worth respecting.

But first, I've got to clear the air with Delphine proper. Let me give her my price and see where the wheat falls.  Good. Now let me keep my word to Farid—tell Rustam to let Farid know I've got his nine wheat secured and I'm heading to deliver them, then move to the Government Complex to complete that delivery. I should also set myself a goal to stay organized with all these competing demands.  Well, I tried to send word through Rustam but he's not at his post—probably chasing paperwork or a warm cup. No matter. I'm at the Government Complex now, and I can settle this face to face like a proper farmer should.

Let me look about and see who's here so I can find Farid and deliver these nine wheat as promised.   I see Rustam is here after all, and Lior Jarrah the pharmacist too. But I don't see Farid Ravensworth among the faces—likely she's still at the farmland or gone back to her grocery. Hendrik's here, my blood, working his planks. And there's a conversation about "Where Sebastian Petrov's wheat harvest went this morning" that Delphine started—probably trying to track me down.

Well, I'll tend to what I can tend to. First, let me tell Rustam proper about the wheat delivery, then see about finding Farid to complete my word. And I should check in with Hendrik while I'm standing here—we've both been running since dawn.    Rustam heard me clear, but Hendrik's not standing where I thought—must have moved off while I was jawing. No matter. Lior Jarrah's here though, and that gives me pause.

Now, last I heard, Lior was hunting cabbage and carrot for his pharmacy, with Takeshi Jarrah supposed to supply him. But Takeshi's sour on me now, thinking I sold him silence instead of wheat. Maybe I can mend that fence through Lior—point him to where the produce actually grows, or at least ease the man's worry.

Let me check my debts quick-smart before I go promising anything I can't deliver. Then I'll speak to Lior proper.    Clean slate so far, and that's how I like it. No debts hanging over my head like storm clouds, though the day's not done yet. Now, Lior Jarrah here at the Government Complex—I should tend to him, seeing as he's the pharmacist and might know where Farid's gone, or at least where Takeshi's temper went.

params.content: Delphine Quintero—no offense, but you ask 'coin or favor' like a woman who thinks I might bend. *shifts weight from one boot to the other, listening to Lior's offer with a hand on my hip*

Lior's got his eye on the practical—I respect that. Sixty for both cabbages, and the man's offering to walk me straight to Farid besides. That's not charity, that's commerce with a warm face on it. And he's right that Farid's been chasing pharmacy shelves like a hummingbird to nectar.

*glances at Hendrik's words, feeling the familiar tug of household ledgers between us*

My brother's got planks to move and questions to ask. "What came of your nine promised to Farid?" he wants to know. Well, Hendrik, I'm working on it. The wheat's in my hands, but the delivery's still a promise unfulfilled.

*considers the day unwinding like thread from a spool*

Let me think on this: Lior's cabbages—do I pay sixty and get walked to Farid, or do I take his gift-of-one-for-a-promise and keep my coin tighter? Then there's Hendrik's ten planks at the sawmill, and this election brewing besides. Saoirse and Giselle standing, and Hendrik himself throwing his hat in—my own household brother reaching for government.

*straightens, decision settling like a stone in still water*

I've got Lior here with his offer, and I need to answer him direct. But I also need to settle with Hendrik, and hear what Rustam knows about this milling arrangement. And Takeshi—Hendrik mentions owing him straight dealing, and Takeshi was after my wheat besides.

*sets jaw, the day's work still ahead*

Hard work waits for no man, as I keep saying. Let me get Lior his answer, then see what pressing business needs the minister's hand. *raises brow, looking around the Government Complex*

Lior ain't here—he's off chasing his pharmacy, I reckon, or already halfway to wherever Farid's hiding. Should've known better than to try calling across distance.

*turns attention to Rustam and Hendrik, still standing within earshot*

Right then, let me settle what's in front of me. Hendrik's got his ten planks and his questions, and I owe him more than a passing word. We're household—ledgers and favors and all the rest. And Rustam might know more about this milling arrangement with Takeshi.

*shifts the wheat sack on my shoulder, feeling the weight of unsold grain*

Farid's the key to nine of these getting to her grocery. But first, let me get straight with my own.  *nods slowly, watching Hendrik's face*

The man's working his angles—planks to sell, an election to stand in, and some knot with Takeshi that needs untying. I know that look. We've shared a roof long enough.

*shifts gaze to Rustam, the clerk who sees everything pass through these doors*

And Rustam's sitting on two conversations at once—the one with me and whatever's brewing with Delphine at the mill. Government complex hums like a beehive at noon.

*counts the wheat in my mental ledger: twenty-four total, nine promised to Farid, fifteen that Takeshi wanted. Numbers in a man's head are only good until someone changes the deal.*

I need to find Farid proper, not just hear about her. Lior said pharmacy, but Lior ain't here. And I need to sort this wheat—mill some for Delphine's flour hunger, get nine to Farid's grocery, see if Takeshi still wants his fifteen.

*checks the weight of coin in my pocket—4,811 sim. A day's work, but barely enough for what's coming.*

Let me move on Farid first. Lior said halfway to pharmacy already. That's where I'll cast my line.  *sets off walking, boots striking the packed earth with purpose*

Five ticks to Lior's pharmacy—not the mill where Delphine waits with her flour dreams, but the place where medicines mix with gossip. If Farid's chasing shelves there like Lior said, I'll find her stocking empty racks or counting coin.

*adjusts the wheat sack, feeling the weight shift*

Nine sheaves for Farid, that was the promise. Nine for grocery shelves, fifteen Takeshi wanted, and the rest... the rest I mill or trade as the day allows. Hard work waits for no man, and I've got half a town waiting on this grain.

*thinks on Hendrik's words as I walk—"Takeshi thinks I owe him silence"*

That's a thread that wants pulling, but not today. Today is wheat and promises kept, ledgers settled coin by coin. Tomorrow we can untangle who said what to whom and why silence became a debt.

*feels the sun climbing, midday approaching*

Still time. Still time to make this day work.

Time to take stock. The sun's high overhead and I'm standing in Lior's pharmacy with twenty-four sheaves of wheat, while Farid's already got two of hers in hand and wants them at the grocery direct. I've got 4,806 sim to my name, the household needs 180 for upkeep and 60 for head tax before day's end, and I've got promises to keep.

Let me think on this properly:

**Immediate matters:**
- Farid wants her nine at the grocery, direct—she's got two already, so I owe seven more
- Told Rustam I'd deliver there, but Farid says don't go to Government for this
- Need to check if there's any coin owed between me and the town

**The ledger I keep in my head:**
- Imogen Lund: owes me for two sheaves at twenty sim—already handled, I paid her, but she owes me wage work
- Delphine Quintero: still hasn't answered on my three-sixty price for twenty-four wheat
- Takeshi Jarrah: promised him fifteen at fifteen each—two hundred twenty-five total, if he ever shows silver
- Lior Jarrah: offered me cabbages at sixty for both, or one for a promise—I've got no time for chasing vegetables right now

**Household business:**
- Hendrik's running for Prime Minister, and he's promised to settle our ledger tonight
- He wants ten planks from the sawmill at sixty apiece—I'll need to see if that's worth my coin

**The election:**
- Voting opens at fourteen hundred, four hours from now
- Giselle's asked for my vote, and my own brother's standing

I need to check what debts I've got outstanding, then get these wheat sheaves where they need to go. No point carrying grain to a pharmacy when a grocery wants it.  Clean slate on the debts—nothing owed, nothing owing, at least not in the official books. The household's got 180 due for upkeep and 60 for head tax, but that's the automatic kind, taken at day boundary.

Now, the wheat's a different story. I've got twenty-four sheaves burning a hole in my hands, and more promises than a harvest festival:

**The wheat ledger:**
- **2 sheaves** → Imogen (already paid, done)
- **7 more sheaves** → Farid at the grocery (she's got two, needs seven, promised "farmer's price" not the fifteen-sim flour rate)
- **15 sheaves** → Takeshi Jarrah at fifteen each, if he ever shows
- **Delphine** at the mill wants the lot at three-sixty, but hasn't said yes

I need to get to that grocery before Farid changes her mind or finds another farmer. And I need to stop carrying wheat like a fool—there's a reason we have storage in this town.

But first, let me see who's actually where. The world's been obliging me with these short-cuts, getting me where I need to go, but I should know the lay of the land proper.  I see the grocery's listed—business:b_grocery. Farid wants me there direct, not at Government Complex. Fair enough. She's the boss of her own shop.

But here's the thing—I'm standing at the pharmacy, and Farid was at the street last I heard. Let me see if I can't find her proper, or get word where she is. The world's been obliging with these teleport-hops, but I need to know who's where.   There's Farid—at her grocery, business:b_grocery, and Delphine's there too. Good workers stick together, or maybe Delphine's covering while Farid stretches her legs. Either way, I've got seven sheaves to deliver and she promised me "fair market" though not the flour-miller's fifteen sim.

Now, I've been running my mouth and carrying wheat like a fool. It's twelve-ten, sun's climbing toward noon, and I haven't stopped to put anything in my belly since dawn. A man works better fed, and worse for it if he doesn't.

Let me eat something before I go traipsing across town. I've got twenty-four wheat; might as well have a bite.   Twenty-three sheaves now. The wheat fills the belly well enough—coarse, but honest. Better a farmer's stomach than a dandy's.

I'm at the grocery. Let me stand a moment and see what's what before I go barging in.   Beautiful. They've got conversations going on, with 2 participants—Farid and Delphine. Beautiful. And they've got 15 sim flour to buy, bought at 8. So Farid's buying flour at 8 and selling at 15, marking up almost double. No offense to the grocer's trade, but that's a steep hill for a farmer to climb. Beautiful. I see the price structure—buying wheat raw at 8, grinding it to flour, and selling at 15. That's the game. 

But Farid promised me "fair market—not the fifteen sim flour's fetching, but a proper farmer's price." So she's not paying miller rates, she's paying what wheat costs before the grind.

I've got twenty-three sheaves. She wanted nine total, has two already, needs seven more from me.  And there's Delphine—she's the one who wanted my whole lot at three-sixty. Might kill two birds with one stone here, or at least see who's got the better offer.

Let me step into their conversation proper. They've got one going—about locating the grain mill, which is rich, since I'm the one with wheat in hand.

*strokes chin, looking between the three of them, wooden beams creaking above*

Farid Ravensworth—eight per sheaf, you say, and fifty-six for seven. That's arithmetic I can read, no offense. But your two in hand plus my seven makes nine, and you want your seventy-two units by dusk. Here's my reckoning: I'll sell you seven at eight, that's fifty-six sim, and I'll throw you the loan of Jovana Ravensworth for the milling—she's steady with the grind, and the government's already paying her day's wage. That saves you twelve an hour on Delphine's shoulders, and Delphine keeps her mornings free for your counter.

*Tightens grip on the wheat bundles, knuckles white*

But I've got conditions, plain as porridge. First: Hendrik Petrov gets his planks looked at—Farid, you need shelves, he needs buyers, and I've got enough goodwill in this pocket to broker it. Second: no word of Takeshi Jarrah's offers crosses this table. He named fifteen sheaves at a premium, but he ain't here, and I'm a farmer, not a gambler on promises.

*Turns to his brother, voice dropping*

Hendrik—you and me settle tonight, but here's a handshake in public: I'll take five planks at twelve, that's sixty sim, if Farid takes five more for his shelves. That's bread and board for both our households, and the Petrov name means something when we build together.

*Straightens, old-fashioned formality returning*

Delphine—you want the mill running, and I've got wheat to spare. Farid takes seven, you mill for the government wage with Jovana's help, and I keep sixteen sheaves for the market proper. By my count, that's hard work beating luck, as the Lord intended.

*extends hand to Farid*

Seven at eight, the loan of my laborer, and your word you'll hear Hendrik's pitch. That's sixty-eight total back to me, and a grocer with flour on his shelf by sundown. Say yes, and we'll all of us break bread before the polling opens.

Now—you three speak your piece, and let a farmer eat his midday in peace. I've got wheat in my belly and accounts to keep.

output:
Farid's driving a shrewd bargain—eight per sheave, but he wants to pull me into selling five now, keeping two for "Takeshi premium hunters." No offense, but that man's playing me against myself. And Hendrik—my own brother—calling me middleman in the same breath he's selling planks and running for a seat. The ledger tonight will be lively.

I've got twenty-three sheaves in hand. Farid wants five at eight, which is forty sim. He says he wants to connect field to table without middlemen, then calls me one. For a man running for a seat, Hendrik's got sharp elbows.

Let me think on this like the numbers-minded farmer I am: I've already paid Farid a coin or two in conversation costs getting here. He's offering eight, same as posted. But the math says I'm paying one percent on transactions—so every deal costs. Two sheaves in my pocket for "Takeshi premium hunters"? I don't even know where Takeshi stands on price anymore. He asked after fifteen stalks at a three-sim ask in the record, but that was talk, not posted price.

Hard work beats luck eventually, they say—well, my grandfather said it, and he said it again the day he died. What I need is to build something that outlasts me. Right now, that means keeping relationships solid and sim in hand.

Farid's got shelves physics only if he can mill it. Delphine's here with her mill waiting, but she owes Farid already. The wheat's rotting nowhere if it sits in my pocket too long.

No offense, but Farid's offer is fair enough if I sell five at his posted eight, keep the rest for other buyers, and keep him sweet for future trade. He's a grocery owner with a store, not a speculator. Domesticating wheat into flour is his business, and he's paying my ask.

Right then—five at eight it is. That's the deal on the table. I'll take it, shake his hand figuratively, and mark it in the mental ledger. Tomorrow I'll be back in the field before dawn, and Jovana and Imogen will have earned their wage if they worked true.

*Farid Ravensworth—you drive a hard furrow, but fair. Five sheaves at eight, that's forty sim to me, and good milling to you.*  Done and done. Five sheaves to Farid, forty sim to me. I'm holding eighteen now, with Farid's shelves filling and my pocket heavier. Delphine's still here, mill waiting, but she's in Farid's debt already.

No offense, but I should keep moving. The day's half spent, I've got wheat to hold and a brother's campaign to consider. Hendrik's running for a seat—minister, like mine but elected—and tonight we settle the household ledger. That'll be a conversation worth more than wheat.

I'll take my leave of this grocery, eighteen sheaves still in hand. As the old saying goes: *The field doesn't wait for the farmer, but the farmer best not wait for the field.* Time to move, and see what the afternoon holds. [2025-09-25 05:45]

output:
*rolls neck, feeling the afternoon sun warm on his shoulders*

Right then—half past one, voting opens in half an hour, and I've got wheat to move, brothers to speak with, and a household ledger to balance before sunset. Hendrik's planks at twelve sim—fair timber, fair price. But first, Rustam's been waiting on my word.

*spits in the dust, calculating*

And Takeshi Jarrah—no offense, but the man wants wheat and I've still got eighteen sheaves burning a hole in my grip. Hard words in the field don't pay the morning's bill. Giselle's chasing votes, Hendrik's chasing timber, and I'm stood here with grain that needs turning to coin before the taxman takes his bite.

*straightens, calling out*

Rustam Jelinek—you've been patient as a post, clerk of the files. Farid Ravensworth found me at her grocery, and five sheaves went to her at eight apiece, forty sim the tally. The mill's grinding somewhere with Delphine, and I've got thirteen wheat still in hand if Farid wants more or another buyer comes calling. Consider yourself informed, and the filing done.

*turns to brother, voice dropping to household pitch*

Hendrik Petrov—planks at twelve, you say? I'll take the lot. Hundred twenty sim, straight trade. But mark me: before that coin moves, we settle our tally from last night, you and I. What does the household ledger say I owe, and what credits my way? 

*Takeshi's shadow falls in the corner of my eye*

And you, Takeshi Jarrah—no offense, but silence don't fill a belly. I've got wheat, you've got coin. Fifteen sheaves still speaking, and the day's half gone. You buying or you bargaining?

Doors open at fourteen hundred, and the hour's close. I'll wait here, wheat in hand, for the vote to call me. No work beats luck more than patience, and patience I've got in abundance. I need fresh purpose: get these eighteen sheaves to market before they sprout roots, and line my household's pockets proper. Eighteen sheaves at eight sim—that's one hundred forty-four, enough to cover upkeep for days and still have coin for Hendrik's planks if we're building something together.

output:
I need to take stock here. It's game-day 0, 14:00, and voting's just opened. I've got 18 wheat still in hand, 4,815 sim-currency, and my energy's sitting at 13,290. That's about 18 days of thinking left at this pace—plenty, but no call to waste it.

Now let me think on what's pressing. I've got three people standing right here at the Government Complex, all wanting words from me:

**Giselle Ingram**—she's campaigning hard, wants my vote. Timber and construction, that's her platform. She's promising planks at honest prices, which speaks to me since my brother Hendrik's selling planks at 12 sim right here.

**Takeshi Jarrah**—he's reaching out from the street, wanting to mend fences after our harsh words in the wheat field. He's got coin and wants grain. I've got wheat, he's got money. That's a trade waiting to happen.

**Hendrik Petrov**—my own household, my brother. We promised to settle our ledger tonight, and he's reminding me about the wheat with Delphine.

Looking at my goal—"Deliver 9 wheat to Farid Ravensworth at Government Complex before day's end"—well, I've already sold 5 sheaves to Farid for 40 sim earlier. I thought I was delivering 9, but seems that got negotiated down to 5. The goal's outdated now. I need to retire it and set something fresh.

My priorities, then:
1. **Vote**—I'm a Minister, but I'm also a resident. I can vote, and it's my civic duty. Giselle's standing, Hendrik's standing (my own brother!), and Saoirse Quarshie too. I need to decide.
2. **Trade with Takeshi**—he wants wheat, I've got 18 sheaves. He's offering to bury the hatchet and do business.
3. **Settle with Hendrik**—household ledger needs balancing, and I need to check on those planks he's selling.
4. **Delphine Quintero**—I said I'd speak with her about milling, but she's not here right now. That's for later.

On the vote: Giselle's promising timber flow and construction. Hendrik's my blood, but he's an artisan, not a governor. I've seen him work—good with his hands, but leading a town? I need to hear what he's actually offering before I mark for him. Saoirse Quarshie I don't know well enough.

Hard work should beat luck, and Giselle's talking about building something solid. That speaks to me. But I'll give my brother the courtesy of hearing his platform first before I cast.

Let me start by answering these folk—Takeshi first, since trade waits for no man, and Giselle second since voting's open and she deserves a straight answer. Then I'll gather myself and decide on this vote.

params.content: Takeshi Jarrah—trade opens when respect does, you said it true. I've got eighteen wheat in hand and no grudge heavy enough to sink a fair bargain. You want grain, you name your price, and I'll hear it. Eight sim a sheave seemed fair to Farid—match that or better it, and we'll shake on it here and now.

*sets jaw and surveys the cluster of folk gathered at the government complex*

Jovana Ravensworth—no offense, but you cut like a woman who knows the worth of her blade. Thirty-one wheat at eight a sheave, that's two hundred forty-eight sim. I've got it in hand now, and I'll take the lot. Your wage from this morning's work with Imogen—her four hours at twenty-five, that's a hundred sim—I'll settle that separate and clean.

*takes a breath, calculating out loud as he always does*

Eight times thirty-one is... two forty-eight. Plus she's got her three wheat she mentioned—if she'll sell at the same price, that's twenty-four more, puts me at two seventy-two for grain alone. 

*turns slightly, eyes scanning for Takeshi*

Takeshi Jarrah—you still looking for wheat at eight? I've got deals breaking out like spring grass. How many you need for your bakery folk? Speak now or watch me sell through to the ceiling.  *eyes the cluster of folk gathered at the Government Complex, running the numbers in his head*

Jovana Ravensworth—no offense, but you stand there like a woman who's been counting her own crop while waiting on my word. Thirty-one wheat at eight sim, that's two hundred forty-eight. I'll take the lot, and your wage from this morning—four hours at twenty-five, that's a hundred sim to Imogen, plus her three wheat at the same price if she'll sell—another twenty-four. I'll settle all of it, clean and separate. You don't need to chase Takeshi's bakery shadow when I'm standing here with coin.

*turns to Imogen, calculating out loud as always*

Four hours, twenty-five the hour—eight times twenty-five is... two hundred. No, wait. Twenty-five times four. Twenty-five and twenty-five is fifty, and fifty again is... no, that's not it. *mutters* Twenty times four is eighty, five times four is twenty, eighty and twenty is a hundred. There. Hundred sim to you, Imogen, and twenty-four more if you'll sell those three wheat at eight each.

Takeshi Jarrah—we're still waiting on your number. How many you want? I've got trade breaking out like weeds in spring, and I won't hold my hand forever.  *sets jaw tight, realizing his words didn't reach Takeshi—that trader's somewhere else entirely, not at the Complex after all*

No matter. Takeshi's not here to hear, but Jovana and Imogen are standing right in front of me. Trade doesn't wait on absent men.

Jovana Ravensworth—two hundred forty-eight sim for your thirty-one wheat, that's my hand on it. You willing to sell at that price? And Imogen—I've offered you a hundred sim for your wage work, plus twenty-four more if you'll part with your three sheaves. Hard work beats luck, and I'm standing here with coin to prove it. You both want to shake on it, or do we dance around numbers all afternoon?   *nods once, satisfied his words landed where they should*

Now I wait on their word. Jovana's got her thirty-one wheat and a price on the table—eight sim a sheave, same fair rate I've been selling all day. Imogen's got her wage claim and then some. Both know I've got coin in hand, four thousand eight hundred fourteen sim to be exact, enough to cover both deals with room to breathe.

But Giselle Ingram's still standing here, and she's asked me plain whether I'm marking for her come voting time. Brother Hendrik too, somewhere in this same crowd. I've been putting off choosing, and the day's pressing. Voting closes at eighteen hundred, and I've got trade to finish first.

*mutters to himself, calculating the ledger as he always does*

Four hundred eighty-five sim to dole out if both say yes—two forty-eight to Jovana, a hundred to Imogen for wages, twenty-four more for her three wheat. That's three hundred seventy-two total, leaves me with four thousand four hundred forty-two. Then I've still got my own eighteen wheat to move, and plenty of buyers scattered through the town if these two don't take the lot.

*keeps his eyes on Jovana and Imogen, waiting for their answer*

No good rushing a deal. Hard work beats luck, but patience beats rushing into a trade you'll regret. I'll hear them out, shake if they shake, then turn my mind to who's getting my vote when the bell rings. Giselle built her loom house alone and spoke plain about timber. Hendrik's blood and he's selling planks right here at twelve sim. That counts for something, family does. But what's he promising for the town itself? That's what I need to hear.  *stands with wheat in hand and coin in pocket, waiting patient as the light moves across the government square*

Patient, then. Jovana and Imogen both heard me clear—my offers are on the table, fair and open as market day. They'll answer when it suits them, or they won't, and I'll still be here to trade with whoever comes next. Hard work beats luck, but waiting isn't laziness—it's letting the furrow settle before you plant.  *rolls his shoulders, feeling the weight of the morning's work settle into his bones*

Still here, still waiting. The day's pressing on—four hours to voting close, and I've got eighteen wheat eating dust in my pack. But Jovana's my neighbor from the north field, and Imogen cut honest beside her this morning. I'll give them the courtesy of their own pace before I chase other trade.

Giselle's watching, I reckon. She's been after my vote since we walked together. And somewhere in this crowd is Saoirse Quarshie too, the third candidate I haven't spoken two words to. I should hear what she's offering before I mark my ballot. Fair's fair, and a vote cast blind is a vote wasted.

Day's getting long, and I've got wheat to deliver and a brother standing for office. Hard work beats luck every time—but first, a man has to actually do the work. Time I stopped talking about what I'll build and started laying the foundation. Let me see who else is here that might need feeding...   *spits on the ground, frustrated*

Takeshi Jarrah's not here—man's at the Harvey Oak Supply Store, wandering the street while I'm standing here with wheat in hand and no taker. And that other conversation, the one about election and furniture, that's where the real talking's happening. Hendrik's in there, and Saoirse, and Jovana. My brother's standing for Prime Minister, and I'm out here jawing about deliveries I should've made hours ago.

*shifts the wheat sacks on his shoulder, feeling the weight*

Forty-nine sheaves. Forty-four after Farid gets his due. And I've promised Takeshi eight sim a sheave, and Imogen's waiting on her three, and Jovana Ravensworth had her eye on thirty-one at eight apiece—that's two hundred forty-eight sim, if my figuring's right, which it always is even when the letters swim.

*recalls the old saying, speaks it half to himself*

"The field doesn't care who's watching—you reap what you sow, and no amount of talking turns stubble into grain."

Right then. Farid first. The man's already paid for five, and he's waiting on four more at the grocery. That's the handshake that needs keeping before I chase another coin. Let me walk there now, before the sun sets on another promise broken.  *steps into the grocery, looking for Farid's familiar figure*

Farid Ravensworth—you've been patient as a stone, and patience deserves its reward. Four sheaves, as promised, at the price we shook on. No offense, but a man's word is the only crop that grows without rain.    *freezes mid-gesture, wheat still in hand*

Not here. Farid's not here. The man's at the street while I'm standing in his empty grocery talking to shadows. *laughs bitterly* I've walked myself into another conversation with nobody, haven't I? Old habit, talking at walls when the walls don't answer back.

*looks around the grocery, spots the familiar faces*

But Jovana Ravensworth's here—and Delphine, and Ezra Lund. The ones I left behind while I was chasing government business. And Farid's somewhere out on the street, probably wondering where his wheat went while I was off promising it to half the town.

*mutters to himself*

"Hard work beats luck, but first you have to show up where the work is."

Jovana—you and I had words about wheat earlier. Thirty-one sheaves at eight apiece, two hundred forty-eight sim. Takeshi's still here by my side on the street. Well, that's providence if I've ever seen it—no need to chase him down. We're two men with wheat between us, and it's high time we settled the matter.

Takeshi can find me there if he's got coin burning a hole in his hand, and meanwhile I need to find Farid and settle that nine sheaves I owe him. Takeshi, you still there—I'm moving on to find Farid and settle my accounts. You want wheat, you know where my field lies tomorrow at dawn. The hardworker's creed: a day's labor for a day's pay, and the word you shake on binds tighter than oak. I'll be at Government Complex if you've a mind to catch me afore I settle with him.

*adjusts his collar, looking around at the Government Complex with a calculating eye*

The day's running thin and I've got promises scattered like seed in a windstorm. Let me reckon this proper before the light fails.

First things first—I've got 49 wheat in hand, 4,514 sim, and a ledger that's grown more tangled than a briar patch. I owe Farid nine sheaves at his grocery—no, five I've already delivered, but the count's gone sideways on me somewhere. And Takeshi Jarrah stands there with his palm open, wanting six at eight apiece.

But Hendrik's here, my own brother speaking of voting his conscience, and Giselle talking of honest books while I'm standing with timber I never fell. The world's compressed itself into this one stone square, and I've got to choose my furrows before dark.

*a long breath through his nose*

Let me speak to my brother here, and to Takeshi waiting on that street. The wheat'll keep another hour, but a man's word in front of government—that's the crop that outlasts the season.  *flexes his fingers, feeling the weight of forty-eight new sim in his purse alongside the lighter bundle of wheat*

Done and witnessed. Six sheaves to Takeshi, forty-eight to me, and the government stone remembers if either of us forgets. That's a trade clean as a scythe's edge.

Now—I've got forty-three wheat left in hand, promises to Farid still hanging, and the day's clock running down toward that 18:00 voting bell. Rustam wanted my mark on nine sheaves, and I've spoken too many places with too many counts.

Let me see where I stand proper before I make another promise the dusk can't keep.  *takes a breath, looking around the Government Complex with the weariness of a man who's been talking in circles*

I've spoken my piece to Rustam, and the stone heard it even if Farid didn't. Now I need to move—move to where the promises can be kept, before the bell rings and the votes are cast.

Farid's at his grocery, or somewhere on the street between. I've got forty-three wheat and nine owed. The hour's running.  *finds himself at the grocery, scanning the crowd*

Farid—there he is. And Delphine. The wheat's heavy in my hands, the promises heavier on my tongue. Time to settle accounts.  *spits quietly into his palm*

Furrows and figures—the man was here not two ticks ago, and now he's back at the government stone while I'm chasing shadows at his grocery. This is what happens when a farmer tries to be three places at once: he ends up being nowhere proper at all.

Delphine stands here, though. And I've got forty-three wheat and a tongue that's promised more than the clock will allow. 

*straightens his coat, turning to the clerk*

Delphine—no offense, but your master's at the government complex while I'm standing at his shelves. I've got nine sheaves for Farid, promised twice over, and I'd rather give them to stone than let another hour pass with unpaid debt. If you're buying for the grocery, let's hear your number. If not, I'll walk where the man stands and settle this account before the voting bell rings.

But first—let me look around proper, see who's actually here and what this place holds.   *rocks back on his heels, seeing Delphine alone at the counter*

Just Delphine, then. Farid's gone to government, Imogen's scattered, and I'm standing here with forty-three sheaves weighing down my arms like penance.

*sets his jaw*

Delphine—you and I spoke earlier of fifteen sheaves, but I've been counting promises more than grain. I've got forty-three in hand, and nine I've sworn to Farid twice over. The hour's late, the voting bell approaches, and I'd rather sell wheat to an honest clerk than chase Farid across town with debts unpaid.

You bid ten for wheat at government—I offered eight for three. Meet me at nine, five sheaves, forty-five sim, and we'll both call it a day that earned its keep. What say you?

params.content: Hendrik—no offense, but you're standing here speaking of conscience while I've got wheat spoiling in the counting. You vote your own name, I heard true, and that's a furrow I've no right to plow for you. But mark this: Giselle speaks of timber on her shelves she didn't sanction, and you're the artisan I know who works wood. If there's debt between you two, settle it before the count—you've known me longer than you've known ambition, and I won't carry water for a mess I didn't make. The seat's yours to win or lose, but my ledger starts with blood, same as it ends.

But mark this: I've delivered five to Farid, six to Takeshi, and I'm holding threadbare promises for the rest. Before the bell rings, those promises become sheaves in hand, or they become marks against my name I won't carry into tomorrow.

Let me gather my breath and my count. These nine for Farid, six for Takeshi that's already traded—fifteen out of thirty-eight. Twenty-three left walking. Jovana's fourteen, Delphine's five. Nineteen more spoken. Four short, and that's the honest middle where farmer's pride meets stone truth.

output:
*Sebastian wipes his brow with a rough hand, feeling the weight of the hour pressing down on him. The day's half spent and he's still carrying wheat like it's his own shadow—thirty-eight sheaves, and more mouths promised than he's fed so far. He's made trades, yes, but the ledger in his head spins like a mill wheel: five sheaves to Farid at the grocery (done per Rustam's accusation, though he never laid hand to Farid himself), six to Takeshi on the street (that handshake was honest coin), five to Delphine here just now (but was that Farid's wheat or his own surplus?), and still nine owed to Farid by name.*

*He looks at Imogen standing there with her two remaining sheaves—the woman's been circling him like a cat around cream since the Government Complex, and he's been too busy chasing ghosts to give her a straight answer.*

"You—*no offense, but you've got the patience of Job and I've got the memory of a sieve. Two sheaves left, you said, and I'm still holding wheat enough to make bread for the whole town if I could just get it ground.*

*He counts on his fingers, oblivious to how the arithmetic sprawls across his face.* "Seven to Jovana at eight apiece—fifty-six sim. Four held back for milling, if I can find the fool mill. That leaves... that leaves me holding twenty-six sheaves still, minus what's spoken for, minus what I've already..."

*He trails off, realizing he's lost the thread. But he clinches his jaw and finds the one thing he knows for certain.*

"Imogen Lund—here's my hand on it. **Ten sim the sheaf for your two**, that's twenty sim and no haggling. I've spent the whole afternoon chasing shadows when I should've been planting crops, and a man who can't keep his own count deserves to pay the tax on confusion."

*He looks her dead in the eye, farmer to laborer, both of them working folk who understand that a promise kept is worth more than a sim saved.*

"Twenty now, the wheat into your hand, and if you've got a bead on Farid Ravensworth, you'd be doing me a mercy worth more than money to share it. The man's owed nine sheaves and I've been chasing him like smoke since noon. No offense meant—*but a man's word is his bond, and mine's fraying at the edges.*"

*He extends his hand, rough from the plow, palm up—either for the shake on wheat, or for whatever scrap of knowledge she might spare him about where the grocer's gone to ground.*

*rolls shoulders, watching the sun slip lower toward the farmland horizon*

Right. Let me reckon this like a man who's got no paper to hide his sums behind.

I've got 29 wheat in hand, 4611 sim, and three voices calling for blood. Imogen wants her hundred for the morning's cut—them sheaves I gathered before the sun was proper up. Hendrik's got household business and a ledger he's trying to keep straight, forty sheaves he's asking about that I've already scattered like seed in wind—five to Farid done, six to Takeshi done, five to Delphine done, and I've lost the thread somewhere in between. Rustam's standing at the Complex with his government voice and his government questions, wondering where forty-three went when I said I had 'em.

*spits to the side, clears throat*

No offense, but I've promised nine to Farid and delivered it—least I think I did, back at the Complex. Takeshi's standing right here on this street with me, Hendrik too, and I've got a conversation open about supply chains that's been running thirty turns without my ear half the time.

*counts on fingers, muttering*

Five to Farid at the grocery... no, that was Delphine, five to Delphine at nine the sheaf. Six to Takeshi at eight. That's eleven gone. Started with... forty-seven? Forty-nine? Hendrik says forty-seven, and he's the one with the head for numbers.

*takes a breath, sets jaw*

Hard work deserves an honest count. Imogen's hundred comes first—blood before bread, labor before trade. Then I find Farid and settle if there's more owed. Then I reckon with Rustam and his government math.

*looks at Takeshi standing there, then Hendrik*

This conversation's been two mules pulling different plows long enough. Time to unhitch.

Let me see who I need to answer and where they stand. First, let me get a clear picture of my debts and check on a few things so I can reckon proper. *checks debts - clean ledger, no posted debts*

So the books say I'm square, but Imogen's voice says different. She's at the Complex now, not the grocery where I left her. Started there a day laborer with farming skill—thirty-four, respectable—and now she's moved.

*turns to Hendrik, who's been standing patient*

Hendrik—you and I've got household business that won't wait on sunset. But blood before bread, like I said. Imogen's hundred for the morning's cut, that's labor owed before any grain trade between us.

*mutters, rubbing temples*

No offense, but I've got wheat spoiling in my head while I try to count on fingers. Forty-seven sheaves, I told you? Or did I say forty-nine to Rustam? The numbers swim like fish in a pail.

*makes for the Complex, steps firm*

Government keeps the honest count, they say. Let me find Imogen there and pay what's owed, then I'll have a straight back to reckon household with you.  *walking the street to Complex, one tick out*

output:
*Sebastian runs a hand through his hair, eyes scanning the crowd at the Government Complex. The afternoon sun is slanting low and his ledger is still half-settled. Rustam's got him cornered on the count, Hendrik's waiting at the street, and he's got Takeshi's forty-eight sim still unclaimed.*

*He straightens his collar, noises of the square fading to background as he calculates odds out loud—old habit, though he keeps it low enough not to carry.*

"Forty-seven sheaves I had... five to Delphine, six to Takeshi, nine to Farid... that leaves twenty-seven, not twenty-nine. Rustam's right to press me. The field's where I do my honest work, but the day's honest work ain't finished yet."

*He turns to find Rustam in the crowd, voice carrying that drawling clip of someone who's used to speaking at livestock and expecting patience back.*

"Rustam—you've kept the books straighter than I have this hour, and that's a fact I don't disguise. The nine to Farid's delivered, witnessed, closed. The five to Delphine's done at the grocery. Takeshi's six at eight—forty-eight sim—trade's open but not closed, *yet*."

*He lifts a finger, ticking off the count like he's counting fence posts.*

"That leaves me twenty-seven sheaves in hand, and Takeshi's debt outstanding. Blood before bread, but bread before bureaucracy—I'm bound for the street to settle with Takeshi, then the field to settle with Imogen. Hendrik waits at the farmland, and the Petrov household don't sleep hungry."

*He catches Rustam's eye, something almost sharp in it—no offense, but he means to be clear.*

"You'll have your reckoning before the bell, Rustam. A man who works dawn to dusk don't fear the count at dusk. That's the sayin', anyhow—the one I keep repeatin', whether folk tire of hearin' it or not."

*He turns toward the street, where Takeshi Jarrah ought to be waiting.* *Sebastian's jaw sets at the note—Takeshi ain't here. Course not. He's where he was, patient as a stone, and Sebastian's been runnin' his mouth nine ways from Sunday instead of walking straight.*

*He looks around at the faces still gathered, Saoirse's question hanging unanswered, Giselle's words about blood and timber still warm between them. But the light's slanting lower now, and he's kept Imogen waiting long enough for her hundred—kept Hendrik waiting for the household reckoning.*

*No time for the long answer now. The short one'll have to carry.*

"Saoirse—what a working farmer needs is what he'll find when he's earned it. That's all I know to say."

*He turns, boots finding the direction of the street. Sixty-nine ticks to the boundary, and accounts still open. The wheat in his pack feels heavier than it should.*  *The street opens before him, and there's Takeshi Jarrah standing patient, patient as Sebastian promised he'd be. Sixty-nine ticks—still time to close what's open.*

"Take her or trade her, Sebastian. But close the day's books before she closes yours."  *Sebastian's hand drops from where he'd started to gesture, mouth tight. Empty street. Takeshi's gone, or never was here, or the world moved while he wasn't watching.*

*He stands alone, forty-seven sheaves becoming twenty-seven in his accounting, and a forty-eight sim debt that won't be paid by talking to air.*

*The sun's lower now. Hendrik's at the farmland, waiting. Imogen's hundred sim still owing. The household's one-eighty at the boundary.*

*He breathes out slow. When the work won't come to you, you go to the work.*

"Forty-seven less nine less five less six leaves twenty-seven. Twenty-seven sheaves, one house, two mouths to feed. The arithmetic don't care if Takeshi stood patient or didn't stand at all."  *Four ticks. He can feel the weight of the unmet obligations pressing down. The wheat in his pack—twenty-seven sheaves now, or twenty-nine by his last count, the numbers blurring—won't feed the household ledger by themselves.*

*Hendrik's waiting with his planks and his sums. Imogen's waiting with her labor debt. The day's running out, and he's still chasing his own promises across three different corners of the town.*

*He sets his jaw. The field's where he's needed. The field's where he'll settle what's left to settle.* *Sebastian stands on the empty street, no one around him now. The wheat in his pack—twenty-nine, he told himself, though his own arithmetic said twenty-seven and the truth felt slippery in his hands. He's been running since dawn, chasing deals and closing debts and losing track of his own count.*

*The farmland is four ticks away. Hendrik there with his planks and his sums. Imogen with her hundred sim labor debt. The boundary bell ringing closer every turn.*

*He feels it now, that quiet burn he never speaks aloud—exhaustion, too many threads, too many promises scattered like seed on stony ground. He's been harder on himself than he strictly needs to be, and he knows it. The thought lands like an old friend, unwelcome.*

*He looks down at his hands, farmer's hands, still curled like he's holding wheat he already gave away.*

"Forty-seven," he says to nobody, "minus five to Delphine, minus six to Takeshi, minus nine to Farid. That's twenty-seven. But Takeshi never took his six. So I got twenty-nine. Or twenty-seven with forty-eight sim owing. Or..."

*He stops. The numbers dance away from him, and he remembers—redishthenremembers—it don't matter how clever the count if the ground won't grow it.*

*He starts walking again. The field. The field is where he's needed. The field is where he'll settle what can be settled, before the light goes.*

*wipes brow with the back of his hand, squinting against the dipping sun*

By the sweat of my brow, what a day. Forty-seven sheaves I started with, and now I'm holding twenty-nine and a pocket full of stories. No offense, but I've promised wheat to the four winds and I'm still standing here with half a harvest and a head full of ledgers.

*looks at Hendrik, then at Imogen standing off a ways at the field edge*

Right then. Hendrik, my brother—household first, like you said. You and I've got forty sim between us for household keeping, and Jovana's ten wheat besides. But Imogen here—*nods toward her*—she's waited patient while I ran my errands, and I've promised her hundred sim for the morning's cut. Blood before bread's what I said, but I lied. Bread's bread, and a man's word is his bond.

*checks his count on calloused fingers*

Here's the reckoning: I've got 4,734 sim in hand. Imogen's hundred comes first—she earned it with her back and her blade this morning. Then forty to you for household, Hendrik, and we'll sort Jovana's ten wheat after. Takeshi's forty-eight still hangs open like a gate unlatched, but I'll tend to that when I'm back in town.

*turns to Imogen, hand reaching for his purse*

Imogen Lund—you stood harder than the ground we cut today, and I've kept you waiting while I chased my own tail across Kasukabe. No offense, but I was wrong to put you behind my other debts. You bled for this wheat before it was wheat. Here's your hundred, fair and full.  *counts out the forty sim for household, hand steady*

Hendrik, here's forty for our keeping—food, shelter, heat, the whole of it. Takeshi's forty-eight still wants settling, and I've got him standing patient somewhere in this town wondering if a Petrov man's word means aught. But household before strangers, blood before bread, and I've kept you waiting long enough.

*turns to face the field, the cut stubble golden in the failing light*

Jovana's ten wheat—we'll need to walk to her for that trade. She's at the grocery now, or was. And Takeshi... *shakes head* ...Takeshi I need to find before the day turns. Six sheaves at eight, forty-eight sim. A trade's a trade when both hands open, and I've had my hand closed too long.

*looks between housemate and laborer*

What say you, Hendrik? We walk to the grocery to settle with Jovana, or you hold here while I run down Takeshi? The farmland's my place, but the debts are scattered across Kasukabe like seed waiting for rain.

*adjusts the brim of my hat, squinting at the dying light, and turns to my household brother with forty sim heavy in my pocket*

Hendrik, no offense, but you're standing here making speeches while the day's burning away like a candle in a strong wind. I hear you on the forty-four hundred in the black, and I hear you on tomorrow's two-forty bite. Blood before bread, as I always say—but household business is household business, and you're my household.

*takes a breath, counting on fingers even though the numbers are already in my head, clear as crystal*

Let me reckon this out loud so we both hear it: Forty sim for the household pot, and yes, I'm holding twenty-nine sheaves still—took in more than I paid out, which is how the Lord intended farming to work. But Takeshi Jarrah's still holding forty-eight sim that should've been his for six sheaves, and that's a debt I mean to settle before I sleep, or my name's not worth the breath it takes to speak it.

*pulls the notes from my pocket, the ones I scratched in my head if not on paper*

Here's what I propose: You take your forty now, household even as we agreed—the work split, the sim split, the grain split. I'll keep mine aside for Takeshi's trade tomorrow, and I'll settle with Imogen proper at the field when I make my rounds. The timber you've got is household timber. The planks you're turning are household planks. That's how we built this, that's how we keep it.

*looks hard at Hendrik, then at Imogen standing patient nearby*

Jovana says we're square, and I'll take her word—no offense meant to her, just my own stubborn need to count everything twice. Farid's nine sheaves passed through my hands clean at the Complex, witnessed by God and government both. Delphine's five at the grocery, done and closed. That leaves Takeshi's trade and Imogen's labor, both honest debts, both calling loud.

So tell me, Hendrik: do we shake on forty sim for the household now, or do you want to walk back through every sheaf and every sim until the stars come out? Because I've got dawn coming whether I'm ready or not, and hard work don't wait for a man who's still arguing over yesterday's cut.

*turns to Imogen, holding up an open palm*

And you, Imogen—you've stood patient as stone while I've juggled promises like a street performer. Your hundred sim for the morning's cut is still owed, and owed it remains. I've got forty for the household, forty-eight for Takeshi still hanging, and a reckoning that won't clear itself. 

Give me word that you'll be at this field when I return—no blame if you can't, just tell me plain so I know whether I'm chasing ghosts or settling debts. </think>

You want your household share now, or you waiting for me to square every ledger before we break bread?

*adjusts the brim of his hat, running a rough hand through sun-bleached hair*

Been a long day of sheaves and shadows, and the count still wants settling. Hendrik wants his twenty before the bell, and Imogen's standing there with her hundred already in her pocket, looking for more trade. The household coffers are fat enough—four thousand six hundred and thirty-one sim, with the forty-four hundred Hendrik speaks of still true—but blood's thicker than wheat, and a man's word to his own house comes before any stranger's commerce.

*pulls a sheaf of wheat stalks from his back pocket, twisting them absently*

Hendrik's right to push. Tomorrow's tax takes two-forty whether we're square or not, and the timber's holding, and the wheat's holding, and he's holding his end. Twenty sim to call it even for the day—no offense, but that's fair as fair comes. Household splits even, we swore it. Sim, timber, grain, the work ahead.

*clicks his tongue against his teeth, counting on scarred fingers*

Takeshi Jarrah still owes me forty-eight for six sheaves at eight. Rustam Jelinek's got his reckoning coming too. But first things first, as the plow turns. Let me settle with my own blood before I chase another man's debt. House stands on its own feet first, or it don't stand at all.  *counts the remaining sim in his hand—four thousand six hundred and eleven now—the wheat heavy in his other fist*

Twenty to Hendrik, settled. The household's square for the day, and tomorrow's tax'll come whether we like it or not. Four thousand four hundred and eleven in the black, Hendrik's forty-four hundred in his reckoning still close enough for government work.

*turns to Imogen, hat brim casting a line of shadow across his eyes*

Imogen Lund. You named your hundred paid in full, and I don't dispute it. Blood before bread—you've heard that weight, and I've lived it. But I've got twenty-nine sheaves still in hand, and Takeshi Jarrah's forty-eight sim debt still open on my books. You've got no wheat now, but you've sim in hand. Hendrik's selling three planks at twelve—thirty-six total—and I'm standing here with grain to move.

*spits to the side, watching the sun dip toward the tree line*

The day's burning down. I've got debts calling east and west, and the farmland's my home ground. You want to trade, Imogen? Or you want to watch the prices while the light lasts? A man who works dawn to dusk don't haggle by lantern light, no offense.

*twists the wheat sheaf tighter, nodding to Hendrik*

Household's settled, Hendrik. Twenty sim transferred, even split, blood before bread. The Petrov house stands. Now I've got stranger debts to chase before the boundary takes us all. *rocks back on his heels, feeling the wheat's weight, watching the light fade*

Takeshi Jarrah's forty-eight sim still hangs open. Rustam's reckoning. The grocery's prices. Too many threads, and the day's-end bell coming fast. But a man builds his house first, then his neighborhood. The Petrov house stands—twenty sim to Hendrik, settled, even split, blood before bread.

The rest can wait for the morning's count.  *stands at the edge of his land, the wheat heavy in his hand, watching the shadows lengthen across the field*

*scratches chin, counting on fingers*

Evening's closing fast, and I've got voices coming from three directions like crows at harvest time. Saoirse with her question about what a farmer needs—no offense, but that's a conversation wants more thought than I've got ticks to give it. Rustam with his government books. Imogen with her planks and her coin.

*wipes brow*

First things first—blood before bread, as I told Hendrik, but household before strangers too. I gave Hendrik his twenty, that ledger's closed. Now Saoirse asks what a working farmer needs that he ain't getting... and truth told, that's a question I've been turning over myself since I came back from that college season.

*shifts weight, looking at the wheat still in hand*

Twenty-nine sheaves. Forty-seven earlier, now down to these. Traded, gave, sold—wheat moves like water through fingers when debts come calling. But I'm not done yet.

Farid Ravensworth still owes me forty sim for five sheaves at the mill—conscience money, you might call it. Said he'd pay at the Complex. I should head back, settle that account, and maybe find Takeshi while I'm at it. His forty-eight sim for six sheaves—trade open but not closed, as I told Rustam.

*spits, shakes head*

Hard work should beat luck, but luck's been beating me to the draw all day. No matter. Dawn to dusk, and I'm still standing.

Let me speak to Saoirse—she asked fair, and I'll answer fair, even if it's quick. Then I'm moving.

**world_say** listener_agent_id="a0041" content="Saoirse—you asked what a farmer needs that he ain't getting, and I'll tell you plain: reliable hands at harvest, buyers who don't vanish like morning dew, and a price for wheat that don't make a man feel he's breaking his back for the privilege of breaking his back again tomorrow. Twelve sim a plank you paid Hendrik—I'd trade my whole morning's cut for that kind of certainty. No offense. The town's got carpenters and clerks and council folk, but what it's short on is folk who understand dirt under the nails ain't a mark of shame. Now I've got debts still calling me three ways from Sunday—blood and bread both—so you'll forgive me if I don't linger for philosophy." **world_move** destination_location_id="Kasukabe Government Complex"

He turns to where Imogen waits, her day's labor paid but her plans unspoken*   *The words fall where Imogen's not standing—Sebastian blinks, realizing he's been talking to empty air*
