output:
I been runnin' myself in circles all day, and that's a fact I plain admit. Hendrik's got his forty sim, Imogen's got her hundred for the mornin's labor—paid before the clock struck nineteen, mark me on that. Takeshi's trade came through at last, six sheaves for forty-eight sim, though the trade tool had other ideas about it.

Now I'm standin' on my own farmland with twenty-nine sheaves still heavy in my hands, and the day's near done. No point callin' out to absent ears—Ezra's drifted, Imogen's gone, and I'm alone with the wheat and the ledger in my head that don't do nobody no good if I don't speak it proper.

What I need now is to see where I stand before the boundary hits and the house automatics take their cut. Household of two, the taxman says—Hendrik and me—forty for the head tax, one-eighty for the keepin'. I got forty-six and sixty-four in hand. Light goes at twenty-two hundred, and I'm tired, but the work's not done 'til the book's square.  The books are clean, as Rustam would have it—nothin' owed, nothin' comin'. But that's debts formal, and I keep a tally informal, the half-jokin' kind between kin and household. I'm owed the truth from my own memory, not from any ledger the government keeps.

I'm tired. Thirteen thousand energy and change, but the day's been long and my feet know it. Wheat in hand, coin in pocket, and the farmland quiet around me. Hendrik's planks wait at the mill, Giselle's construction yard sits with timber and planks both—seven planks at fifteen, if I needed 'em.

But what I need now—no offense to myself—is to rest where I stand and let the evenin' settle. The tax won't wait, but the tax is paid for in time I've already spent, in sim I already earned. Forty sim for the household, and I've give Hendrik his half. Dawn to dusk, and I still got an hour before the dark.

I'll rest a moment. Think on what to build that outlasts me, as I swore I would. Somethin' in this town besides the tally I keep in my head, where every favor's accounted and every debt remembered 'til the day we settle it genuine.   The farmland holds me. Empty now, the day's workers gone to their own hearths and their own reckonings. Wheat heavy in hand—twenty-nine sheaves, more than a man eats and less than a market makes. I've sold nine to Farid, six to Takeshi. Fourteen gone, and still enough to speak of.

I think on what to build. Not houses—I ain't got the land for buildin', nor the permit, nor the capital. Not a business—I know the land, not the ledger. But somethin' that outlasts me. A reputation, maybe. The man who works harder and longer than he needs to, and knows it. The man who keeps his word when the tools fail and the trade goes sideways. The man who pays before he's asked, and asks before he takes.

Or maybe just a better way to work this land. The harvest tool's got its limits—farmland:wheat, not Kasukabe Farmland generically. I've learned that today, paid the cost in energy and time to walk where I should've started.

I've been runnin' since dawn, and I've run myself near to empty. But the work's honest, and the day's been true. Forty sim to Hendrik, hundred to Imogen, forty-eight from Takeshi. Nine to Farid at the government, witnessed proper. The household's square, and tomorrow'll need its own earnin'.

I'll stand here in the quiet, holdin' wheat, 'til the boundary comes and takes its cut automatic. Then sleep, then dawn, then work again. That's the rhythm. That's the promise I made to myself when I came back from that college season, provin' what I still ain't quite proved.     The dark comes slow this season, and I'm glad for it. Time to stand still, which I don't give myself often enough—burn out quiet and never say so, that's my way, 'til I collapse. I've said that to no one, and I won't. A man who works dawn to dusk don't complain about the weight of the day.

Twenty-two hundred approaches. The automatics will take their two-twenty—forty tax, one-eighty keep. Hendrik and me, two mouths, two debts to the household ledger. I've give him his share, and mine'll go automatic from what's left. Forty-six sixty-four minus whatever the day spent in move and say—I'm runnin' thin on the margins, but I'm runnin' honest.

The farmland stretches empty. I could walk to the grocery, see if Delphine's still there from my earlier trade. Could walk to the mill, speak with Hendrik proper about tomorrow's work. Could walk to the government, try to catch Rustam for that reckoning I promised him—though he's likely gone to his own rest by now, and I'll owe him the truth of it come morning.

Or I could stay. Be still. Let the evening settle and the boundary come.

I choose the stillness. Hard work don't always beat luck, I know that resentful, but tonight I'll take what luck gave—wheat in hand, roof overhead, and a partner who knows the value of an even split. The Petrov household don't sleep hungry. That's enough for now. That's enough 'til dawn. I been standin' still too long, and the system's noticed. That's a habit I ought to break—restin' when I should be movin', thinkin' when I should be actin'. The boundary's close now, twenty-two hundred near, and I've got wheat in hand that won't harvest itself nor sell itself neither.

What I need is purpose for the evenin's last ticks. I've got twenty-nine sheaves, enough to feed a household or trade for coin that feeds it better. I've got forty-six sixty-four sim, enough to weather the automatics but not enough to build that legacy I'm chasin'.

The election's comin'—game-day one, candidacy closes ten o'clock. I could declare, I suppose. Stand for somethin'. But I've not the head for governin', nor the patience. I know the land, not the law.

Or I could walk. To the mill, speak with Hendrik about tomorrow's planks and what we'll build with 'em. To the grocery, see if Delphine's still mindin' the counter and wants more wheat from my surplus. To the government, settle that reckoning with Rustam I promised—though he's likely gone, and I'll owe the mornin' for it.

The farmland's quiet. Empty. Mine, for this moment, 'til the day ends and the new one begins with its own demands.

I choose to walk. Not rest, not think, but move. To the mill, where Hendrik works, where the household's other half earns his keep. We'll speak of tomorrow, and what we build together. That's the legacy worth chasin'—not stone, not wood, but the work between kin that outlasts the worker.     The mill takes me sudden, no road between. That's the way of this town—places touch places in ways the eye don't follow, and a man walks in memory more than in mud. I'm here now, where Hendrik works, where the planks stack and the saws sing their song.

I look around, see who's present, what the evening has brought to this place of craft and labor.
